english_text: They were bad. One time she said, “This man’s wife was running around on him. The old woman sat in front of the fireplace and put all she had down. And there, the boy saw she had laid out some arrowheads. She had hung what they call a moccasin––you know the kind made out of deer skin––she hung it in front of where she had the arrowheads. Later on, she left and one of the arrowheads made a sound, so she went to where the bundle was on the chimney. Later on, when she came back, she said to the flint, “You didn’t do anything.” So then she sent another arrowhead and again when it came back it hadn’t done anything. “You didn’t go do anything either,” she said to it. Then she put it away. When the third one left and came back she had a container this [gestures] size with water, and the arrowhead went into it. It was washed, and the arrowhead had blood on it. “You really did something,” she said to it, then she put it up. Later on, someone came and told the boy that his wife had died at the dance. The flint must have shot her.

syllabary_text: ᏍᏓᏱᏛ ᎠᏗ ᎠᏎᏃ ᎠᏯ ᎨᎲ Uh
english_text: Well how I see it, it is going to be difficult for us. Because it’s coming as the older ones predicted already. Also, they say we are going to lose our language, and I believe that is going to happen. And someday the money we are using will not be of any use for us —that’s what the older ones said too. And the gardening —if you don’t know how nothing will grow (famine will happen), even if you don’t know how to hunt, or make a garden. This Walmart that we have today—when Covid-19 happened it was hard on everybody, especially those that don’t know how to cook. McDonald’s wasn’t open, cause some people that’s all they know, they don’t know how to cook. They would go get something to eat and they are the ones that it will be hardest for. They don’t know how to grow things; they just go get something. Also, like the deer— something that’s provided for us, something will happen, so we won’t be able to eat them anymore. So really, we are going to see hard times. Me, I feel sorry for my grandkids. I think about my grandma all the time. She used to scare me. I believe what she said, she was sorry for my kids. I was probably about eight years old; she was crying. I said, “What’s wrong with you? What’s going on?” “It’s going to be hard times, and your kids, and their kids are going to go through a hard time,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going to have kids because I don’t even like girls,” I told her. “You will have kids,” she said. “Cause you’re a man, you will have kids.” I still think about all that they said, my grandpa, my dad’s dad. My grandpa didn’t raise my dad. His aunt was the one that raised him. They took us to Grandpa’s house and my dad knew that they didn’t raise him. After Dad had his kids, they started talking some. That’s where we all gathered, at Grandpa’s house, and that’s what he always said, “It’s going to be difficult.” But I wasn’t listening to what the elders said. When I’m home by myself, I try to remember what they said when they spoke about the future. I wish I had listened, I’d rather have played ball with all my cousins. My grandma used to sit outside—that’s when I began to want to play baseball. I guess I was about five or six years old. I wasn’t playing yet at Sallisaw—that wood my uncle carved (uwelvsv) and the blue jeans that we are wearing today, my grandma used to cut and stuff them, then sewed them up to make balls. That’s what we had for balls. We had two and that’s what we were using playing ball, when somebody hit it too hard it tore up. And my grandma was sitting there. When it broke, she would sew it right back up. And then we started playing again. She had one of them there by her and, when, if this one broke, she would throw that other one in. I guess that’s how much she enjoyed watching us play ball. We always played ball there, and Grandma would sit on the porch watching us and laughing. That’s what I remember the most —that we played well, and because we never had fights. We never went anywhere looking for trouble while we were playing ball. I guess Grandma, she enjoyed that.

english_text: Well how I see it, it is going to be difficult for us. Because it’s coming as the older ones predicted already. Also, they say we are going to lose our language, and I believe that is going to happen. And someday the money we are using will not be of any use for us —that’s what the older ones said too. And the gardening —if you don’t know how nothing will grow (famine will happen), even if you don’t know how to hunt, or make a garden. This Walmart that we have today—when Covid-19 happened it was hard on everybody, especially those that don’t know how to cook. McDonald’s wasn’t open, cause some people that’s all they know, they don’t know how to cook. They would go get something to eat and they are the ones that it will be hardest for. They don’t know how to grow things; they just go get something. Also, like the deer— something that’s provided for us, something will happen, so we won’t be able to eat them anymore. So really, we are going to see hard times. Me, I feel sorry for my grandkids. I think about my grandma all the time. She used to scare me. I believe what she said, she was sorry for my kids. I was probably about eight years old; she was crying. I said, “What’s wrong with you? What’s going on?” “It’s going to be hard times, and your kids, and their kids are going to go through a hard time,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going to have kids because I don’t even like girls,” I told her. “You will have kids,” she said. “Cause you’re a man, you will have kids.” I still think about all that they said, my grandpa, my dad’s dad. My grandpa didn’t raise my dad. His aunt was the one that raised him. They took us to Grandpa’s house and my dad knew that they didn’t raise him. After Dad had his kids, they started talking some. That’s where we all gathered, at Grandpa’s house, and that’s what he always said, “It’s going to be difficult.” But I wasn’t listening to what the elders said. When I’m home by myself, I try to remember what they said when they spoke about the future. I wish I had listened, I’d rather have played ball with all my cousins. My grandma used to sit outside—that’s when I began to want to play baseball. I guess I was about five or six years old. I wasn’t playing yet at Sallisaw—that wood my uncle carved (uwelvsv) and the blue jeans that we are wearing today, my grandma used to cut and stuff them, then sewed them up to make balls. That’s what we had for balls. We had two and that’s what we were using playing ball, when somebody hit it too hard it tore up. And my grandma was sitting there. When it broke, she would sew it right back up. And then we started playing again. She had one of them there by her and, when, if this one broke, she would throw that other one in. I guess that’s how much she enjoyed watching us play ball. We always played ball there, and Grandma would sit on the porch watching us and laughing. That’s what I remember the most —that we played well, and because we never had fights. We never went anywhere looking for trouble while we were playing ball. I guess Grandma, she enjoyed that.

And the last week of the fourteenth month I got a telegram in Japan saying she was very sick. syllabary_text: ᎯᎸᏍᎩ Ꮫ ᏄᏓᎴᏒ ᏓᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ ᏥᏫᏄᏥ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᏩᎴᏅᎲ
english_text: I worked at a few different places when I was a young man. I started working at Cookson Store for a while. George Stratton was the name of the owner. His wife's name was Helen, they were good people, very friendly. I worked there for a while and then that big water came and they closed it, then they started building on the water. Boat docks they called them, for boats, and then someone from Ft. Smith came and started building some like that there at Cookson Bend was the name there. He found out I was working, and he came to Cookson, “I will pay you more if you help me build those boat docks,” he told me. “We will see what happens, I help my friend out here,” I told him. “We will talk about it. I can't go with you right away. If I can give him a week or two weeks' notice that I am going to quit, then I will go,” I told him and he agreed so that is what I did and went to build where they put boats, boat docks. He had a little store, and I worked there and then I worked there for about two years and that store owner at Cookson, his son, a young man, he was building all the way around that lake you would call it. “Did you build those building at the lake?” he said. “Yeah, I helped,” I told him. “I am not building on the water I am building on the mountain,” he told me. “I want you to help me,” he said. “This really is my house where I walk and work,” I told him. “Don’t think anything. No mistake, I can meet here at the store and leave from here in the mornings. We will go around building. A meeting place will be at Cookson,” he said. “I will give him a week notice to find someone else to help him, I can't just quit,” I told him. So, I went and helped him for a week at a time, sometimes for longer. I was building around there on the water and then when we finished all those houses around the lake there is just a few buildings we did not build. And when we finished there, St. Claire Lime Company, Sallisaw then they called me and said you can help us. I have never made white dust before.“ You will not be making any, you can just watch the workers. If they are doing good or not, you will be sitting up high. There are stairs, you can sit up high on the second step, you can show them what to do,” he told me. “I don’t know if I can show them what to do, I have never done that before. I have never made lime before,” I told them. We are going to tell you what to do, you just have to watch the meters and when you watch the meters there were several of them and when you watch the meters, they got to hold at a certain degree. All 24 hours, they can't go up, they can't go down, they got to stay right there. “I can do that,” I told him. “I know you can do it,” that boss told me. Then I started there and worked for a long time. I was working there when I went into the Army, when I got out and finished the Army, where did I start then?

His wife's name was Helen, they were good people, very friendly. I worked there for a while and then that big water came and they closed it, then they started building on the water. Boat docks they called them, for boats, and then someone from Ft. Smith came and started building some like that there at Cookson Bend was the name there. He found out I was working, and he came to Cookson, “I will pay you more if you help me build those boat docks,” he told me. “We will see what happens, I help my friend out here,” I told him. “We will talk about it. I can't go with you right away. If I can give him a week or two weeks' notice that I am going to quit, then I will go,” I told him and he agreed so that is what I did and went to build where they put boats, boat docks. He had a little store, and I worked there and then I worked there for about two years and that store owner at Cookson, his son, a young man, he was building all the way around that lake you would call it. “Did you build those building at the lake?” he said. “Yeah, I helped,” I told him. “I am not building on the water I am building on the mountain,” he told me. “I want you to help me,” he said. “This really is my house where I walk and work,” I told him. “Don’t think anything. No mistake, I can meet here at the store and leave from here in the mornings. We will go around building. A meeting place will be at Cookson,” he said. “I will give him a week notice to find someone else to help him, I can't just quit,” I told him. So, I went and helped him for a week at a time, sometimes for longer. I was building around there on the water and then when we finished all those houses around the lake there is just a few buildings we did not build. And when we finished there, St. Claire Lime Company, Sallisaw then they called me and said you can help us. I have never made white dust before.“ You will not be making any, you can just watch the workers. If they are doing good or not, you will be sitting up high. There are stairs, you can sit up high on the second step, you can show them what to do,” he told me. “I don’t know if I can show them what to do, I have never done that before. I have never made lime before,” I told them. We are going to tell you what to do, you just have to watch the meters and when you watch the meters there were several of them and when you watch the meters, they got to hold at a certain degree. All 24 hours, they can't go up, they can't go down, they got to stay right there. “I can do that,” I told him. “I know you can do it,” that boss told me. Then I started there and worked for a long time. I was working there when I went into the Army, when I got out and finished the Army, where did I start then?

english_text: What? Oh yeah, I went back to the lake. Six-shooter was the name then I started there for a very long time, about 18 years. Then Cherokee Nation found out I was working there fishing; we had a fishing dock where people could go to fish. They found while they were there, the Chief, Ross Swimmer and someone named Bobby was with them. I was working there. They came, “We need your help,” they said. “You need my help? To catch a big fish, I'm going to have to take it out of the lake for you.” “No Charley, we bought Burnt Cabin, Burnt Cabin Marina, we want you to come over there and run it for us and fix it up. We need to fix it up really good, and you got this place fixed up good. We want that place fixed up that good.” “Well, I been working for this guy, helping this guy many years, about 18 years, I can't just walk off and quit.” “Think about it,” Ross Swimmer told me, “Think about it, we sure need help over there, we got people working over there rebuilding that place, but when they get off that dock it lays over.” It does! Yeah “what will make it do that?” he said. “They are not doing it right, that is why it is doing that. That’s why we need your help,” he told me there."You will be working for the Nation, Cherokees”, that is what I am. “Well, I will tell my boss what I am going to do, I got a boss here somewhere I will tell him, give him a notice, I can't just walk off and leave,” I told Ross. “Ok think about it,” he told me, when you make up your mind let us know.” OK, that was the end of that. Just the next morning he called back again, that one that was named Bobby was with Ross, came back. “Charley, have you thought about it?” “What do you think, what are you talking about?” “Helping us on that boat dock!” “I ain’t had time to think about it yet. I been doing some things I can't just stop and start thinking!” I told him. “Well think about it, you got to come help us,” Ross said when he came back the second time. Okay, I will be there about four or five days from now, got to let this guy know so he can have a replacement. When I went there, they really did have a broken-down building; we fixed it back up there. They had some workers from here they said were carpenters, but they did not know how to build on the water. They would be learning then. We started, but all the people were gone that had boats there. Because it was run-down, they did not want to stay in a run-down place. They were already gone, so I helped them. We fixed it up. I had been there about a month, and it was full where you put the boats. The buildings were standing good. I worked there for about a year. Ross and the one that was with him came and looked around to see what was going on. He said, “Charley, we sold this place.” “After all this hard work I went through fixing this place you already sold it!” I told him. Yeah, ok I barely got the keys out to use there. “Here are the keys,” I told him. “No, I can't do that, I got to let that guy come in first.You can show him around.” “Well, I ain’t got no job now since you sold this place.” “You just stay here till that guy comes.” “Ok,” I told them. He did come there in about two weeks. I gave him the keys, “Here is the keys. This key here fits that, and this fits that and that over there, and the cash register is right there. Here is the key to the cash register. I don’t know what they are going to do about that money, I don’t know whose money it is.” He got it, he made an agreement with Ross now. I didn’t have a job about two or three weeks; I still didn’t have a job.

english_text: What? Oh yeah, I went back to the lake. Six-shooter was the name then I started there for a very long time, about 18 years. Then Cherokee Nation found out I was working there fishing; we had a fishing dock where people could go to fish. They found while they were there, the Chief, Ross Swimmer and someone named Bobby was with them. I was working there. They came, “We need your help,” they said. “You need my help? To catch a big fish, I'm going to have to take it out of the lake for you.” “No Charley, we bought Burnt Cabin, Burnt Cabin Marina, we want you to come over there and run it for us and fix it up. We need to fix it up really good, and you got this place fixed up good. We want that place fixed up that good.” “Well, I been working for this guy, helping this guy many years, about 18 years, I can't just walk off and quit.” “Think about it,” Ross Swimmer told me, “Think about it, we sure need help over there, we got people working over there rebuilding that place, but when they get off that dock it lays over.” It does! Yeah “what will make it do that?” he said. “They are not doing it right, that is why it is doing that. That’s why we need your help,” he told me there."You will be working for the Nation, Cherokees”, that is what I am. “Well, I will tell my boss what I am going to do, I got a boss here somewhere I will tell him, give him a notice, I can't just walk off and leave,” I told Ross. “Ok think about it,” he told me, when you make up your mind let us know.” OK, that was the end of that. Just the next morning he called back again, that one that was named Bobby was with Ross, came back. “Charley, have you thought about it?” “What do you think, what are you talking about?” “Helping us on that boat dock!” “I ain’t had time to think about it yet. I been doing some things I can't just stop and start thinking!” I told him. “Well think about it, you got to come help us,” Ross said when he came back the second time. Okay, I will be there about four or five days from now, got to let this guy know so he can have a replacement. When I went there, they really did have a broken-down building; we fixed it back up there. They had some workers from here they said were carpenters, but they did not know how to build on the water. They would be learning then. We started, but all the people were gone that had boats there. Because it was run-down, they did not want to stay in a run-down place. They were already gone, so I helped them. We fixed it up. I had been there about a month, and it was full where you put the boats. The buildings were standing good. I worked there for about a year. Ross and the one that was with him came and looked around to see what was going on. He said, “Charley, we sold this place.” “After all this hard work I went through fixing this place you already sold it!” I told him. Yeah, ok I barely got the keys out to use there. “Here are the keys,” I told him. “No, I can't do that, I got to let that guy come in first.You can show him around.” “Well, I ain’t got no job now since you sold this place.” “You just stay here till that guy comes.” “Ok,” I told them. He did come there in about two weeks. I gave him the keys, “Here is the keys. This key here fits that, and this fits that and that over there, and the cash register is right there. Here is the key to the cash register. I don’t know what they are going to do about that money, I don’t know whose money it is.” He got it, he made an agreement with Ross now. I didn’t have a job about two or three weeks; I still didn’t have a job.

I been doing some things I can't just stop and start thinking!” I told him. “Well think about it, you got to come help us,” Ross said when he came back the second time. Okay, I will be there about four or five days from now, got to let this guy know so he can have a replacement. english_text: Fireplace, that old woman she was kneeling down near there. After a while something made a sound, it seemed like in the fireplace, and went up. english_text: We were doing that every weekend, visiting each other. They would be playing dominoes or playing cards. Sitting there until midnight. The late, Ulud(i) had a ’50 model flatbed truck. He would be looking out of the truck, driving by, this [gestures] would be happening, like it was a plane [his hand]. They would park it—if they rode in the truck. We were visiting each other. They cooked back then—nobody cooks nowadays—as I was growing up, my late aunt, Sil(i) was her name. She was Alits(i)’s wife. Then I grew up and I was working. They worked in Decatur, Alits(i) and his daughter, Didi—they called her Lucinda. When they would leave at three o’clock, then Sil(i) and I would get up. And in the living room, there hanging on the ceiling was where she made quilts. “Kam,” she’d say to me. “Get up!” she’d say. She’d wake me up at three am. She was teaching me how to sew quilts. When I got married, I had seven quilts that I had made myself. My mom was teaching me to cook. “If you don’t ever get married, at least you’ll know how to sew and cook, so you won’t be starving. english_text: Yeah, that’s true. When I was growing up, one time, I was about 16 years old. The lumber yard hired me on. There was a long trailer loaded with lumber. english_text: Also, one time we were talking about him—his name was Gas(i). He was taking a motor out of a truck. He had already taken the motor out, and it was sitting by him. And they pushed him all the way to the store. He went and bought what he needed. And outside there was a bench where the old men sit. Gas(i) got in the truck and he was telling the men that he couldn’t get it to start. “I can’t get it to start,” he said. “Well, we’ll try to push you!” they said. They pushed him going backward. When they got to the road they pushed him again, but it still didn’t do anything. Then after a while, somebody pulled up, “What’s wrong, Gas(i)?” “We can’t get it to start!” he said. “Alright, I’ll push you!” he told Gas(i). They pushed him all the way home. There wasn’t a motor inside it.

english_text: I learned a lot from my dad about raising and killing hogs. And skinning them. That’s who I learned from. He turned it all over to me y’know, to gut it. He turned it all over to me. And shooting them. The first time, “Alright, you shoot it!” he told me. I shot it 17 times. [laughs] The hog was still walking around. It was screaming. “Give it [the gun] here!” he told me. I was probably about 14 years old. I was a little scared to shoot it, but I didn’t mind skinning them. But then he told me to shoot it. He gave something to think about. I also learned to fry hog from my dad. And then my late mother, she’d say, “Alright, you boys!” she’d call us. “You all need to be learning to cook! It might happen. You’ll marry one and might not know how to cook. And when you all have children. If your wife is sick, who’s going to feed them?” That’s what our mom would tell us. “Don’t bring them here,” she’d tell us. I don’t know. But I really do appreciate it now. And I try to live the way I grew up. Like, hominy with squirrel meat mixed in. I learned that from my grandparents. My grandmother’s birthday was in November. She didn’t speak English. But when it was October, she would say, “I hungry squirrel!” That’s what she’d tell us boys. “Y’all go hunt it!” We would kill about 50 or 60 squirrels. We would skin them and Grandpa would put them in the stove to dry them. Then in November there’d be squirrels hanging all over the kitchen! Then in November, they’d get those cast-iron pots, about four of them, they’d build a fire, then they had water boiling. They had hominy cooking and they put the squirrels in with it. We’d be sitting there taking the meat off of the bones, then they’d throw it in the hominy. That was when you’d get full.

english_text: …Tahlequah. I was learning at high school. Three donuts were five cents. And Pepsi was 10 cents. There was three of us and we gathered up 15 cents to buy donuts. And we were sharing the pop. That was our lunch. Then I started playing baseball. I would ride the #8 bus from home to high school. Sometimes the bus would have already taken off, then I’d have to walk seven miles. Sometimes before I’d got out of Tahlequah, somebody that knew me would pick me up. But, I don’t know how many times I had to walk home every step of the way, no ride, and it would get dark. But that’s how it was when I grew up. It was interesting the way I grew up, but I feel good about it. She was in church, but not me. My dad was a leader (singer) at the Stomp Ground. All of us, Dad, Mom, we all gathered at the Stomp Ground at Chewey. I learned to lead dances and to play the drum.

english_text: Well, we had made plans to get married. “Let’s go to the revival!" she told me. It’s at the Indian Baptist Church. So, I went with her, it was on a Thursday night. Really, I didn’t want to go, but I went with her. I heard the pastor preaching himself. I was thinking about when I was playing at a dancehall, instead of listening. That J.R. Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Really, I didn’t want to go, but I went with her. I heard the pastor preaching himself. I was thinking about when I was playing at a dancehall, instead of listening. That J.R. Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Boy, I was standing there looking at the door. It wasn’t no further than that door right there, I was standing. That’s when I decided to get out. I couldn’t do it. When I took a step, I just went toward where Scale was standing. I went through there and he shook my hand. “What is it?” he said. I said, “I need Jesus,” three times. He sat me down. They started shaking my hand. They were crying; the late Winn and the late Hester were both crying. “What did I do?” I thought, standing there. They were hugging me, shaking my hand. And I thought, “What did I do?” When I got up in the morning, I used to shake. My stomach, or my guts, it was just like somebody was ripping them out. That’s the way it was. Then, on the fourth day when I got up, I was going to go to work. It felt like I had lost something, so I started looking in the house. I didn’t know what it was that I had lost. I put a coffee pot on the stove, put coffee and water in it. I used to brew my coffee. Then it came to me: my stomach wasn’t hurting. I looked at my hands and I wasn’t shaking. That was when I felt like I was healed. That's how it was, which was strange to me. It was strange to me. I went to work and I was crying. That’s how it happened, that’s where it [my faith] began. But when Saturday night came, the dance hall where I used to play, I went there and I played. Then when Sunday came, I got baptized. We had a new preacher, it was diganotsah,ld, he’s the one that baptized me. Then, after he baptized me, he said, “Are you going to ask Andy if it’s all right for you to be playing round-up club?” “As long as I don’t drink, it’ll be alright,” I told him. So, I went to the club and we were playing. Boy, something slapped me. I was playing and then [slap!] After it hit, it stung. This is what I heard, “DJ, what are you doing here?” it said. I looked at the clock, it was 9:30pm. Boy, but those two hours, it felt like all night to me. I never felt that lonesome before. But I got lonesome then. Two and half hours, then we finished playing. I put up my guitar, I put it in the case. I told Buddy, “I’m quitting.” “What’s going on?” he said. “I shouldn’t be here in the first place,” I said. “I joined church.” I didn’t know how to tell him that it’d help me to let it go. So, I quit the band. I heard him telling the others, “Give him two months! He’ll be back!” they said. I preached when he died. I just about preached to the whole band members when they died. That’s how it all happened, that’s where it started. It was 1972.

syllabary_text: Quit doing this quit doing that ᎥᏬᎮᎸ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏂᎨᏯ ᎠᏁᎲ ᏧᎾᏁᎵᏛᏅ
english_text: Well, we had made plans to get married. “Let’s go to the revival!" she told me. It’s at the Indian Baptist Church. So, I went with her, it was on a Thursday night. Really, I didn’t want to go, but I went with her. I heard the pastor preaching himself. I was thinking about when I was playing at a dancehall, instead of listening. That J.R. Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Boy, I was standing there looking at the door. It wasn’t no further than that door right there, I was standing. That’s when I decided to get out. I couldn’t do it. When I took a step, I just went toward where Scale was standing. I went through there and he shook my hand. “What is it?” he said. I said, “I need Jesus,” three times. He sat me down. They started shaking my hand. They were crying; the late Winn and the late Hester were both crying. “What did I do?” I thought, standing there. They were hugging me, shaking my hand. And I thought, “What did I do?” When I got up in the morning, I used to shake. My stomach, or my guts, it was just like somebody was ripping them out. That’s the way it was. Then, on the fourth day when I got up, I was going to go to work. It felt like I had lost something, so I started looking in the house. I didn’t know what it was that I had lost. I put a coffee pot on the stove, put coffee and water in it. I used to brew my coffee. Then it came to me: my stomach wasn’t hurting. I looked at my hands and I wasn’t shaking. That was when I felt like I was healed. That's how it was, which was strange to me. It was strange to me. I went to work and I was crying. That’s how it happened, that’s where it [my faith] began. But when Saturday night came, the dance hall where I used to play, I went there and I played. Then when Sunday came, I got baptized. We had a new preacher, it was diganotsah,ld, he’s the one that baptized me. Then, after he baptized me, he said, “Are you going to ask Andy if it’s all right for you to be playing round-up club?” “As long as I don’t drink, it’ll be alright,” I told him. So, I went to the club and we were playing. Boy, something slapped me. I was playing and then [slap!] After it hit, it stung. This is what I heard, “DJ, what are you doing here?” it said. I looked at the clock, it was 9:30pm. Boy, but those two hours, it felt like all night to me. I never felt that lonesome before. But I got lonesome then. Two and half hours, then we finished playing. I put up my guitar, I put it in the case. I told Buddy, “I’m quitting.” “What’s going on?” he said. “I shouldn’t be here in the first place,” I said. “I joined church.” I didn’t know how to tell him that it’d help me to let it go. So, I quit the band. I heard him telling the others, “Give him two months! He’ll be back!” they said. I preached when he died. I just about preached to the whole band members when they died. That’s how it all happened, that’s where it started. It was 1972.

Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Boy, I was standing there looking at the door. It wasn’t no further than that door right there, I was standing. That’s when I decided to get out. I couldn’t do it. When I took a step, I just went toward where Scale was standing. I went through there and he shook my hand. “What is it?” he said. I said, “I need Jesus,” three times. He sat me down. They started shaking my hand. They were crying; the late Winn and the late Hester were both crying. “What did I do?” I thought, standing there. They were hugging me, shaking my hand. And I thought, “What did I do?” When I got up in the morning, I used to shake. My stomach, or my guts, it was just like somebody was ripping them out. That’s the way it was. Then, on the fourth day when I got up, I was going to go to work. It felt like I had lost something, so I started looking in the house. I didn’t know what it was that I had lost. I put a coffee pot on the stove, put coffee and water in it. I used to brew my coffee. Then it came to me: my stomach wasn’t hurting. I looked at my hands and I wasn’t shaking. That was when I felt like I was healed. That's how it was, which was strange to me. It was strange to me. I went to work and I was crying. That’s how it happened, that’s where it [my faith] began. But when Saturday night came, the dance hall where I used to play, I went there and I played. Then when Sunday came, I got baptized. We had a new preacher, it was diganotsah,ld, he’s the one that baptized me. Then, after he baptized me, he said, “Are you going to ask Andy if it’s all right for you to be playing round-up club?” “As long as I don’t drink, it’ll be alright,” I told him. So, I went to the club and we were playing. Boy, something slapped me. I was playing and then [slap!] After it hit, it stung. This is what I heard, “DJ, what are you doing here?” it said. I looked at the clock, it was 9:30pm. Boy, but those two hours, it felt like all night to me. I never felt that lonesome before. But I got lonesome then. Two and half hours, then we finished playing. I put up my guitar, I put it in the case. I told Buddy, “I’m quitting.” “What’s going on?” he said. “I shouldn’t be here in the first place,” I said. “I joined church.” I didn’t know how to tell him that it’d help me to let it go. So, I quit the band. I heard him telling the others, “Give him two months! He’ll be back!” they said. I preached when he died. I just about preached to the whole band members when they died. That’s how it all happened, that’s where it started. It was 1972.

phonetic_text: tohy hena
phonetic_broad: toy ena
english_text: Really, it’s going to be hard times soon. The government is wasting money. They are helping people overseas. If we get fat, he gets onto us. But here, the sick can go for help at a hospital. It’s a really good thing we’ve got going. I have really fussed about some things. These people that sit there and gripe, burns me up. I was sitting there waiting to be called. An Indian man was sitting there, but he wasn’t Cherokee, and he kept fussing around. I got mad at him. “This place is not costing you a thing!” I told him. “It is costing me!” he said. “If you are able to pay, then get out and go somewhere else!” I told him. “I think I can pay,” he said. And then when he said that he got called. There would’ve been two old men fighting, but I don’t know… Then another time, I wasn’t in church then, I was at that old hospital that was by the college. I was sitting there waiting to be called. There was a young man sitting there fussing and cussing around. “The doctors don’t know anything!” he was saying. Boy, it just burned me up! I got up and went to stand where he was sitting. “Just be quiet!” I told him. “It would be best if you just walk out and go home. Someone might get called quicker,” I told him. “If you are griping that much here. They have other doctors’ offices. Just go over there!” I told him. Ms. Carter was working in the E.R. “Tell him again, DJ!” she said [from a distance]. His face turned white. People in the hallway started clapping. I had already had my fists ready. If he got up, I probably would’ve hit him first and he probably would’ve whooped me. But he just got quiet and put his head down. Then Dr. Malabrigo called me. “Was that you who said that to him?” [he asked me.] “Yeah, it was me,” I said. [patting sound] Then he patted me on the back. But really, we don’t have anything to gripe about. They don’t charge us anything. And I get my medicine there; it doesn’t cost me anything. I see a doctor there, but it doesn’t cost me anything. When I go to the doctor, I plan on staying two or three hours.

I was sitting there waiting to be called. An Indian man was sitting there, but he wasn’t Cherokee, and he kept fussing around. I got mad at him. “This place is not costing you a thing!” I told him. “It is costing me!” he said. “If you are able to pay, then get out and go somewhere else!” I told him. “I think I can pay,” he said. And then when he said that he got called. There would’ve been two old men fighting, but I don’t know… Then another time, I wasn’t in church then, I was at that old hospital that was by the college. I was sitting there waiting to be called. There was a young man sitting there fussing and cussing around. “The doctors don’t know anything!” he was saying. Boy, it just burned me up! I got up and went to stand where he was sitting. “Just be quiet!” I told him. “It would be best if you just walk out and go home. Someone might get called quicker,” I told him. “If you are griping that much here. They have other doctors’ offices. Just go over there!” I told him. Ms. Carter was working in the E.R. “Tell him again, DJ!” she said [from a distance]. His face turned white. People in the hallway started clapping. I had already had my fists ready. If he got up, I probably would’ve hit him first and he probably would’ve whooped me. But he just got quiet and put his head down. Then Dr. Malabrigo called me. “Was that you who said that to him?” [he asked me.] “Yeah, it was me,” I said. [patting sound] Then he patted me on the back. But really, we don’t have anything to gripe about. They don’t charge us anything. And I get my medicine there; it doesn’t cost me anything. I see a doctor there, but it doesn’t cost me anything. When I go to the doctor, I plan on staying two or three hours.

syllabary_text: ᎥᎩᏯᏅᏗ ᎠᏭ ᏧᏬᏠᏛ ᎧᏰᎯᎶᏍᎬ ᎠᏫᏄᏥ ᎧᏰᏓᏍᎩᎾᏗᏍᎪᏛ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᎦᎾᎦᏘ Ꮭ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏯᏂᎦᏔᎭ ᏗᏗᎰᏛ Boy
english_text: Really, it’s going to be hard times soon. The government is wasting money. They are helping people overseas. If we get fat, he gets onto us. But here, the sick can go for help at a hospital. It’s a really good thing we’ve got going. I have really fussed about some things. These people that sit there and gripe, burns me up. I was sitting there waiting to be called. An Indian man was sitting there, but he wasn’t Cherokee, and he kept fussing around. I got mad at him. “This place is not costing you a thing!” I told him. “It is costing me!” he said. “If you are able to pay, then get out and go somewhere else!” I told him. “I think I can pay,” he said. And then when he said that he got called. There would’ve been two old men fighting, but I don’t know… Then another time, I wasn’t in church then, I was at that old hospital that was by the college. I was sitting there waiting to be called. There was a young man sitting there fussing and cussing around. “The doctors don’t know anything!” he was saying. Boy, it just burned me up! I got up and went to stand where he was sitting. “Just be quiet!” I told him. “It would be best if you just walk out and go home. Someone might get called quicker,” I told him. “If you are griping that much here. They have other doctors’ offices. Just go over there!” I told him. Ms. Carter was working in the E.R. “Tell him again, DJ!” she said [from a distance]. His face turned white. People in the hallway started clapping. I had already had my fists ready. If he got up, I probably would’ve hit him first and he probably would’ve whooped me. But he just got quiet and put his head down. Then Dr. Malabrigo called me. “Was that you who said that to him?” [he asked me.] “Yeah, it was me,” I said. [patting sound] Then he patted me on the back. But really, we don’t have anything to gripe about. They don’t charge us anything. And I get my medicine there; it doesn’t cost me anything. I see a doctor there, but it doesn’t cost me anything. When I go to the doctor, I plan on staying two or three hours.

phonetic_broad: ayyo tsawatelokwav
english_text: Yeah, I learned it. When was it? When we lived behind the school. One time, I wasn’t there. Anyway, when I got there, “Hey, you have to go down the hill to another building to take a test. If you don’t pass it, you won’t get your certificate," they told me. So, the lady that worked with me, we went down there. “Me, I’m going to go there, but I can’t pass it, because I didn’t know how to read and write.” Because I really didn’t know back then. Anyway, I got there and I told the other woman, “I’m just gonna sit here and wait for you.” – Anyway, “I’m going to pray,” I said. “I’m going to pray real hard,” I told her. So, I prayed and asked God to help me. I told Him, “I don’t know how to read and write.” I prayed for about ten minutes. There was nothing written in front of the paper we were to fill out with syllabary. “If you don’t fill it out, then you won’t pass,” they said. I went and sat down, and the Lord just put everything in front of me. I wrote out the whole syllabary chart. I did this for the next page. I had to read it. You had to write it in English, and also the syllabary, about pages worth. The last page I had to read. Anyway, I just felt funny sitting there writing and I had to read it. “Alright. Thank you, Lord,” I said. I turned in the test paper. Then they called me in. “You did well,” she said. I looked at her, it was Bobbie Smith and Ana [Sixkiller]. They were the ones giving the test. I got 95%. I said, “Oh my gosh! Thank you, Lord!” I said. “What happened to the other 5%?” I asked her. “You went over ten minutes reading it,” she told me. I read it, but I didn’t really know how. That’s when it started, me reading well. I was really glad. If you really believe, the Lord will help you if you ask Him.

english_text: Just right over in the other hollow—Cloud Hollow. Where the church is, up that hollow. Down that way, I was born. We moved around in that area when I was growing up. The last time we moved it was straight from where the church is at the end of the hollow is. Still there—that is where we lived. And when we moved from there “Let's move for good from here,” our dad said. “We are going to travel.” We came across. Grandfather lived across by the hollow little ridge. We came there. And then, “We are moving from this hollow”, he told him. “Why? You all have been living around here a long time.” he said. “That is true. It has to be. I am going to get closer to my work.” And then we came up through the hollow. Dropping things. We came over. Then we went back into another hollow. And, where we came out, there was a little house, close. It was just this wide [gestures]. “We can live there until the summer,” he said. And water and food—there is a creek. “You all can fish there or catch crawdads. And in the evening we will eat good.” We would go there. Norman would follow us all the time. Second— in the family we were half brothers, that one. My dad was his dad, that one. His mom lived nearby. But they moved when we got there. So he stayed with us. He would be with us when we would go to the water. We would go catch lots of fish. We would eat fast, in the evening. He had a sawmill, that boss. My dad worked there. And we would go to the water every day. And then, about two years we lived there, their sawmill broke down. “I guess that’s all for us,” they said. “I guess we will go back, then.” ‘Loaded up and came back up the hollow. We came back down, close to Grandfather’s house. We came back again. [Grandfather said] “That house is still there—where you all lived.” “We are headed back to it,” he said. So, we went back over there. Then they said “Let's make a church on the hill.” They said, “There, before Anigvluyo.” It was flat. And that was our church. We would walk that far. And went there on Sunday or Saturday. At night we would be coming back. And come back there [to the original house]. It was closer for us to go, when we moved there. Then they talked about making a church right there on the hill. “On the ridge,” they said. Then they started cutting wood up, the adults. And was dragging limbs around, clearing for the workers. We made it. My dad’s brother had a sawmill there. He started milling. He milled all that, where that little building is. We made a church there. We went in there. Jen was an old lady then, she would walk using her cane. She would come up. It was like this, there. She would come in on Sunday morning.

english_text: “I really think she was older than that,” I told my brother. “From what I heard, she was 114, they say,” he told me. There is a young man that lives right there. They just rolled her up and got her and put her there. Laid her there just like laying a quilt down. That is how they did it. They laid her.

I said “Did you all catch it?” They just laid down. I was really getting suspicious. It was dark now. We had never been that far. Where I was, there was a good road. I thought “What am I going to do now?” There was a lightning bug flying right there, I caught it. It was shining good light when I held it, and I took its tail off. Mel was little, just little, about yea tall [gestures]. ‘Just now walking good, or she was walking good. The other was bigger. Corene, me, and Arch were adults. We were sitting there. And dad used to hunt all the time. At night time he would be listening, to the dogs he had, that chased coyotes and foxes. He would be listening—Arch and him. They were sitting there, it was dark. “I am going to the woods tonight,” I told him. “Are you going to look for possums?” “I might bring some when I am coming back,” I told him. “OK, watch yourself.” “OK, I will be carrying a light.” I told him. “Ok. ‘Dogs are tied up right there. Take them. They are old, they will not take you very far away.” He told me. I kept walking and came on up. I was walking on a ridge over there. About halfway, where I said, there was a crossroad. About there, I stopped, and the dogs scattered out. They barked way over there. So, I thought “I will just sit right here, at this tree.” There were some places to sit, so I sat down. I was sitting there, listening. When they came up they went that way. They got quite far that way. They might have found a coyote, I thought. I am going to get closer, I thought. And I got up, and I started walking. Somewhere on top I stopped, and I sat down. I was sitting there and the light started getting low. I ran out of coal oil. It got dark. “I guess I am just going to sit here. I have a fire,” I thought. “I am just going to sit here.” They were chasing just over there. They went by, and came back. I said “Did you all catch it?” They just laid down. I was really getting suspicious. It was dark now. We had never been that far. Where I was, there was a good road. I thought “What am I going to do now?” There was a lightning bug flying right there, I caught it. It was shining good light when I held it, and I took its tail off. I stuck it on [my clothes] and then another—they started coming out. I was catching them, putting them on my clothes, and then it was kind of light. Then I started walking. I followed the road. It was clear, right there—they were not going dim. It was good light. That was the way it was. I went off and got back to the house. “I really appreciate you, my God,” I told Him.

english_text: He gave me those to see, to go home with. “I really appreciate you. my God,” I told Him. “I would not have seen anything to think about, if it was not for you,” I told Him. They would go this way,” I told him. ”And then that way.” “Oh, I didn’t hear them,” he said. “I was thinking I better go look for them.” When we got back, I told them I was thankful we had a good time. “I will feed you tomorrow.” I told them. We went to sleep. And then—toward the last—I was going everywhere in the creek. Gigging crawdads [with a small gig spear]. That was it—nothing, nowhere else. Sometimes we made fence posts. Arch would be standing somewhere, sharpening them. And, when he would sharpen them, we would sell them and buy food. We would eat good in the evening. That is what we did all day. Or something. Or the old man would carve railroad ties. If we cut one somewhere, it would be laying there. He would carve it, when he got time. Then he would walk somewhere else, and carve another one. And when he would carve all of them, I would take a horse. I would hook them on, ‘gather them together, and take them up to where a truck would go. We would load them up. We would get them out of the hollow—we would haul them up. Arch would be going around carving posts somewhere. We were doing good. We would kill a hog. Dad would fatten them up, and then we would have food. Just flour, potatoes, and beans—we would buy that. And then we would be eating good. We were not starving. Now’days it is different.

english_text: There was just five of us. My aunt had about 20 kids. She said, “The Bible says go replenish the earth.” I think it was at Cherry Tree, Jerry Nofire said, his wife said, “Yeah, but it didn’t tell you just to do it by yourself.” And his wife was sitting there, and they had about eight or nine kids themselves. Bull is his son. He was a third-generation preacher at Cherry Tree. But Jerry started getting sick all the time, and we knew he was going to pass soon. He said, “Y’all be thinking about who’s going to be preaching for y’all,” sometime around a year before he passed. I was talking to Bull about how he should be the one [who preaches for us], and he said, “I’ve been asking for that for a long time.” We were talking and I chose Bull, and I said, “If you agree to do so, it would be you.” He said, “Let me think about it.” And then he said, “Yeah I will, because we’re going to lose that old man before too long.” And it wasn’t about a year before he really started to get sick and going in and out of the hospital. One time he came back from the hospital, and he got on to us there at church, he said, “You guys here, you’re always praying for me to get better, it’s your fault I’m still here. I’m actually ready to leave.” He was ready to leave, it was because of us praying for him, we were trying to hang on to him. He was ready to leave, that was how he was seeing it, because his wife had already left. “Well, I can’t do anything, I have to pray for you, because that’s what you’ve been teaching us,” is what I told him. We were doing what he told us to do, but he still didn’t like it because he was wanting to go home. One day he went in, they gave up on him, there wasn’t any need for them to know, and he did go home, and then people began to gather at his house. It was like buzzards when they see something laying there. They were eating, and the old man was still hanging in there. We went to visit him, I was doing something at the church, and there was a little girl that came running over to us, she said, “Somebody wants to talk to you,” and I said, “Hang on a minute, let me finish up.” She said, “He’s sitting right there,” and when I went out, there he was after they had given up on him. We talked for a long time, and I said, “What happened?” and he said, “I didn’t feel like going home, so I just thought I better get up.” He was driving that thing that runs by itself, wheelchair. He came to the church, and he said, “I guess they ate everything up, they gave up and went home.” He lasted for about a week after that, and then we were starting to figure it out, that it was close. I visited him every day until the evening, and then one evening I left, I told him I’d come back tomorrow, but first I had to go to town, and it was about 10pm when I got back, and then the phone rang, and he had left.

She said, “The Bible says go replenish the earth.” I think it was at Cherry Tree, Jerry Nofire said, his wife said, “Yeah, but it didn’t tell you just to do it by yourself.” And his wife was sitting there, and they had about eight or nine kids themselves. Bull is his son. He was a third-generation preacher at Cherry Tree. But Jerry started getting sick all the time, and we knew he was going to pass soon. He said, “Y’all be thinking about who’s going to be preaching for y’all,” sometime around a year before he passed. I was talking to Bull about how he should be the one [who preaches for us], and he said, “I’ve been asking for that for a long time.” We were talking and I chose Bull, and I said, “If you agree to do so, it would be you.” He said, “Let me think about it.” And then he said, “Yeah I will, because we’re going to lose that old man before too long.” And it wasn’t about a year before he really started to get sick and going in and out of the hospital. One time he came back from the hospital, and he got on to us there at church, he said, “You guys here, you’re always praying for me to get better, it’s your fault I’m still here. I’m actually ready to leave.” He was ready to leave, it was because of us praying for him, we were trying to hang on to him. He was ready to leave, that was how he was seeing it, because his wife had already left. “Well, I can’t do anything, I have to pray for you, because that’s what you’ve been teaching us,” is what I told him. We were doing what he told us to do, but he still didn’t like it because he was wanting to go home. One day he went in, they gave up on him, there wasn’t any need for them to know, and he did go home, and then people began to gather at his house. It was like buzzards when they see something laying there. They were eating, and the old man was still hanging in there. We went to visit him, I was doing something at the church, and there was a little girl that came running over to us, she said, “Somebody wants to talk to you,” and I said, “Hang on a minute, let me finish up.” She said, “He’s sitting right there,” and when I went out, there he was after they had given up on him. We talked for a long time, and I said, “What happened?” and he said, “I didn’t feel like going home, so I just thought I better get up.” He was driving that thing that runs by itself, wheelchair. He came to the church, and he said, “I guess they ate everything up, they gave up and went home.” He lasted for about a week after that, and then we were starting to figure it out, that it was close. I visited him every day until the evening, and then one evening I left, I told him I’d come back tomorrow, but first I had to go to town, and it was about 10pm when I got back, and then the phone rang, and he had left.

syllabary_text: ᎠᏎᎾᏲ ᎣᏍᏓ ᎮᏅ ᎣᎨᏲᏒ ᎾᎮᏂ salemᎢ ᏣᏁᎭ ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ Ꮲ ᎫᏍᏓ ᎣᏦᏝᎩ ᏱᎦ ᏯᏅᏓ ᎦᏚᏌ ᎣᏤ
english_text: Yeah, he had taught us good. Those people around Salem will tell us, “You guys on the mountain don’t understand nothing,” but we were following the word that was in the Bible, because adulterers can’t get in there. There’s one in there, but he knows, I told him, “You might be the reason good things aren’t happening.” But that girl knows. It was Jerry’s daughter. She tried to take part in the communion, and she was acting like a Christian, but they wouldn’t let her. They told her. “You can come to church here as much as you want, but you can’t take part in the communion.” And she got mad and left for a long time. She was out of church for a long time, but when Jerry passed, she came back and rededicated. But Bull, something happened. I’m not quite sure what happened, I told Bull I wasn’t going to take part in that kind of work. There’s about three of them that don’t need to be in there, but I can’t do anything about it. But one was from another place, Steve Campbell. He’s no good. His wife used to be married. Her husband is still alive somewhere, and that’s no good. Steve Campbell is a licensed minister, and they did take it away. He was at Four Vision's [Baptist] Church, and he left for a long time, and when he came back, he told them he lied to them. He said they had taken his license away but that didn’t stop him from going around and preaching, and even today he still preaches, but not around here. They don’t let him around here, they said he was preaching at some Holiness church. “A Baptist ain’t got no business at a Holiness church,” I told him. That’s what they used to tell us. If a Baptist was preaching at a Holiness church and if that person believes, he will have to go to a Baptist church, not a Holiness church.

english_text: Do you remember those CCFs we used to get? I heard one time that I had a sponsor – where was it? the State of Washington, that it came from. Boy, I heard Nellie Mayes come out of her office. I looked at Watie. He said, “What?” It wasn’t good ‘cause she was walking heavy. I told him, “It’s not good.” She came there in our room. She was standing there. Her son DJ said, “Can I help you, Miss Mayes?” She seen me and pointed. I said, “I didn’t do nothing.” And I didn’t do nothing, so she said, “I need to see Billy in the office.” I told DJ I didn’t do nothing. I grabbed him here [gesture]. He said, “Miss Mayes needs to see you.” So I went in, and as soon as I went in, I said, “I didn’t do anything. I didn’t do nothing wrong.” She said, “I need you to sit down and tell me what this is all about.” She got an envelope out and opened it. And I had never seen a check before. There was a check in there. She said, “Who is sending you money? Why are people sending you money here at school?” I said, “I don’t know. It ain't my fault.” Some people were sponsoring me from Washington. Washington State. There was a 500 dollar check in there, but she didn’t tell me that. She laid it on this side [gesture]. She started to tell me the names of the people – an old man, an old lady, and their daughter. “This is what came with it,” she said. “You tell me what is in this.” Then she pulled out that box. She pushed it towards me. I said, “I don’t want it. I don’t know what is in it. I don’t want it,” I told her. She said, “Open it.” There was a football, a basketball, and clothes in there.

english_text: Tommy Sanders came one time, when we were working at City Lake. My wife said, “Some old man came to visit you in a blue pickup. He needs to talk to you. It’s important.” So I waited. It was about 4:30 in the morning in Baldwin, going towards St. Croix Falls. No houses till like 12 or 15 miles, now there are houses everywhere. We were driving through nothing but cornfields. The corn was this high [gesture]. Out of the east came a car, and it sped up. Out of the west came another. I seen it. We were a way yet. I seen the signal light. It was going to turn where we were coming. Boy, it was coming from the east fast. He sped up his car. I said, “Gaw dernit, Rick! They are going to hit!” Rick heard me and said, “Who’s going to hit?” Soon as he did that, it was early in the morning, dark, no yard lights. All we had was lights on the cars. It just got dark. When they hit, it just turned all the lights out. A girl got killed that morning, so I parked the car on the side of the road and turned on the emergency lights. We ran over there. I went to help the one on this side, the one that got hit, and Rick went to help the one that done it. That girl, you could see that’s how she was laying down. When they hit, she went like this [gesture]. You could see her face that big on the windshield. She hit her head and broke her back. She was killed right there, and the other he was helping was like this [gesture] under the steering wheel. The gear shift was stuck right here. Not through the skull just through the skin it came out here [gesture]. I was trying to open the door so I could help them, but nothing. So I went around. It was pushed against the guard rail, and I could not get in over there. So, I ran back around this way and took my shirt off and wrapped it – I was going to break the window behind them. When I did this, someone said try this door. I had already tried that door. I was going to break the window out. I said, “I done did.” I thought Rick was standing there, and there was nobody else except me, Rick, and them people. So I said, “I done did.” He said, “Try again.” He had been hit right there [gesture]. He was just smashed. The man was in there, moaning. He said, “Tell him you are going to be with him in a minute.” I said, “Hold on, sir, I’m trying to get in to you. Just hold on,” I told him. I grabbed the door, and I done tried this door. The door opened like it was new. And this is God’s honest truth. He knows what I seen. He said, “Get in. He is badly hurt.” He told me to just lean over the seat, but he was talking in English. So I did what he said and followed it. When I grabbed that man, immediately all of my arm turned bloody. I told him what I was going to do. He said, “No, when you bring him back to the seat,” he said, “hold his head. He is really injured. Keep talking to him. Help is already coming.” Who called them? There was nobody. Cars didn’t even go by. So I stayed like that in the back. The blood was going like this here on my hands [gesture], talking to him. I did what the guy asked me to do. I did all of that. Then I seen state patrols. Two of them came. Before that, I seen what the man looked like. He didn’t have a face, and the car was hiding everything of him, but he did not have a face. I seen him. I told him OK. He was wearing red, a red and black shirt. I even put it in the state patrol statement as a witness. I wrote it all down, what I seen. So I told the state patrol. “How long ago did you do this training?” he said. I told him I ain't never done nothing like this. “How did you know what to do?” he said. I said, “That guy out there.” I grabbed him and said, “That guy out there told me what to do.” He said, “What guy?” I said, “There is a guy.” I told him what he had on. They both shined their spotlights and looked around. Nobody was anywhere around. So I said, “Rick, where did that guy go?” I said to him. He said, “What guy, Billy?” I said, “That guy that was just here.” He said, “There ain't no guy, Billy. It’s just us.” By God, he did not have a face. That is what that man told me. Out there, what I did for that man, I talked to him, I told him I wasn’t leaving him. The ambulance came. I was holding him all that time. He said, “Don’t let him go, this man, don’t let him go.” I crawled over the seat and held this man. I crawled over the seat with the ambulance people and they did that to him here. About eight months later, I was sitting at Fall Creek. I had just got back from work. My little girl – the phone rang, and I said, “Don’t answer it.” I was hungry. She quickly answered it. She said, “Hold on. Dad, it’s for you.” Man, I almost cussed. I got to the phone and said hello. They said, “Hello, is this Billy Pettit?” I said, “It’s Billy Pettit.” This is what happened: they said, “About eight months back, I was in a car accident.” Gah-lee, that’s what they said. I was back in that place. I quickly seen that man again. Y’know, there’s a smart—smartass talk… Y’know, he said, “You saved my life.” I almost said, “Did I kill a poop-eating dog?” I almost told him that, but I held my tongue. I said, “Oh, did I? How did I do this?” He said, “I was in a bad car accident. My neck was broke in three places. One bad move and I would have died underneath that steering wheel. You saved my life,” he said. Then I told him what all took place. He said, “Well, I want you to...” He told me his address. He said, “You are our family.” I didn’t even know the man. He said, “I want you to come and bring your family,” he said. “Let’s be as one.” That’s what happened – his neck was broke in three places. What that man said, he already knew how bad he was injured, and today he is still alive and well. Yeah, that’s what I am amazed with. Or I am not amazed. He didn’t have a face. I could not see his face. It was blank, but I seen everything else: his hair was brown, about this long [gesture]. I could see that because I wasn’t parked that far from it. They never found anyone. You can read my statement. I wrote everything I seen that morning.

I will say, “Help the next person, because someone is going to need help.” Because I have had a lot of help in my lifetime and I just want to give some back, yep. There was an incident one time in Baldwin Wisconsin, when I was still living in Wisconsin. Me and a co-worker were driving, he was a machine operator. He had his seat pulled back. It was about 4:30 in the morning in Baldwin, going towards St. Croix Falls. No houses till like 12 or 15 miles, now there are houses everywhere. We were driving through nothing but cornfields. The corn was this high [gesture]. Out of the east came a car, and it sped up. Out of the west came another. I seen it. We were a way yet. I seen the signal light. It was going to turn where we were coming. Boy, it was coming from the east fast. He sped up his car. I said, “Gaw dernit, Rick! They are going to hit!” Rick heard me and said, “Who’s going to hit?” Soon as he did that, it was early in the morning, dark, no yard lights. All we had was lights on the cars. It just got dark. When they hit, it just turned all the lights out. A girl got killed that morning, so I parked the car on the side of the road and turned on the emergency lights. We ran over there. I went to help the one on this side, the one that got hit, and Rick went to help the one that done it. That girl, you could see that’s how she was laying down. When they hit, she went like this [gesture]. You could see her face that big on the windshield. She hit her head and broke her back. She was killed right there, and the other he was helping was like this [gesture] under the steering wheel. The gear shift was stuck right here. Not through the skull just through the skin it came out here [gesture]. I was trying to open the door so I could help them, but nothing. So I went around. It was pushed against the guard rail, and I could not get in over there. So, I ran back around this way and took my shirt off and wrapped it – I was going to break the window behind them. When I did this, someone said try this door. I had already tried that door. I was going to break the window out. I said, “I done did.” I thought Rick was standing there, and there was nobody else except me, Rick, and them people. So I said, “I done did.” He said, “Try again.” He had been hit right there [gesture]. He was just smashed. The man was in there, moaning. He said, “Tell him you are going to be with him in a minute.” I said, “Hold on, sir, I’m trying to get in to you. Just hold on,” I told him. I grabbed the door, and I done tried this door. The door opened like it was new. And this is God’s honest truth. He knows what I seen. He said, “Get in. He is badly hurt.” He told me to just lean over the seat, but he was talking in English. So I did what he said and followed it. When I grabbed that man, immediately all of my arm turned bloody. I told him what I was going to do. He said, “No, when you bring him back to the seat,” he said, “hold his head. He is really injured. Keep talking to him. Help is already coming.” Who called them? There was nobody. Cars didn’t even go by. So I stayed like that in the back. The blood was going like this here on my hands [gesture], talking to him. I did what the guy asked me to do. I did all of that. Then I seen state patrols. Two of them came. Before that, I seen what the man looked like. He didn’t have a face, and the car was hiding everything of him, but he did not have a face. I seen him. I told him OK. He was wearing red, a red and black shirt. I even put it in the state patrol statement as a witness. I wrote it all down, what I seen. So I told the state patrol. “How long ago did you do this training?” he said. I told him I ain't never done nothing like this. “How did you know what to do?” he said. I said, “That guy out there.” I grabbed him and said, “That guy out there told me what to do.” He said, “What guy?” I said, “There is a guy.” I told him what he had on. They both shined their spotlights and looked around. Nobody was anywhere around. So I said, “Rick, where did that guy go?” I said to him. He said, “What guy, Billy?” I said, “That guy that was just here.” He said, “There ain't no guy, Billy. It’s just us.” By God, he did not have a face. That is what that man told me. Out there, what I did for that man, I talked to him, I told him I wasn’t leaving him. The ambulance came. I was holding him all that time. He said, “Don’t let him go, this man, don’t let him go.” I crawled over the seat and held this man. I crawled over the seat with the ambulance people and they did that to him here. About eight months later, I was sitting at Fall Creek. I had just got back from work. My little girl – the phone rang, and I said, “Don’t answer it.” I was hungry. She quickly answered it. She said, “Hold on. Dad, it’s for you.” Man, I almost cussed. I got to the phone and said hello. They said, “Hello, is this Billy Pettit?” I said, “It’s Billy Pettit.” This is what happened: they said, “About eight months back, I was in a car accident.” Gah-lee, that’s what they said. I was back in that place. I quickly seen that man again. Y’know, there’s a smart—smartass talk… Y’know, he said, “You saved my life.” I almost said, “Did I kill a poop-eating dog?” I almost told him that, but I held my tongue. I said, “Oh, did I? How did I do this?” He said, “I was in a bad car accident. My neck was broke in three places. One bad move and I would have died underneath that steering wheel. You saved my life,” he said. Then I told him what all took place. He said, “Well, I want you to...” He told me his address. He said, “You are our family.” I didn’t even know the man. He said, “I want you to come and bring your family,” he said. “Let’s be as one.” That’s what happened – his neck was broke in three places. What that man said, he already knew how bad he was injured, and today he is still alive and well. Yeah, that’s what I am amazed with. Or I am not amazed. He didn’t have a face. I could not see his face. It was blank, but I seen everything else: his hair was brown, about this long [gesture]. I could see that because I wasn’t parked that far from it. They never found anyone. You can read my statement. I wrote everything I seen that morning.

I said, “I done did.” I thought Rick was standing there, and there was nobody else except me, Rick, and them people.
