english_text: Yeah, and long time ago when I was little, I guess I was sick all the time. I remember Mom would put blankets on me when it was hot, trying to sweat it out, I guess. One time I was laying there, Watie was laying on this side. Dad had already passed. I was laying in the middle and Mom on this side. I was laying there with a fever. Someone shined a light in our bedroom. They shined a light. I was laying there, and usually I’ll pull the covers up, afraid of the tsigilis. I was like this, laying there. They shined the light. And I looked at the light. It wasn’t even on, the light, it was so bright in there, the light bulb looked black. It looked burnt. Then I did this [gesture] and thought, “Where is it coming from?” I thought someone was up in the living room. But our bedroom was all lit up. I did this: I got up. It was standing there white against that door. He had his hands like this [gesture], standing there, and I know what I seen. When I tell people, they say you were probably next to death. Near-death experience, they say. No, it wasn’t. I was healed quickly. That was the last time I was sick. So I looked at it. It did not have a face. Again, I seen everything. I didn’t see no nail-scarred hands. He had them like this [gesture]. So I just laid back down. I was doing Mom like this, saying, “Mom” and that light slowly went off. Mom sat up, doing this [gesture], cleaning the tobacco from her mouth. She said, “What, little one?” OK, before I woke up, she was putting blankets on where I was laying or whatever I did. When I woke up, Mom was pressing here on my chest. She was talking to someone, and I didn’t know nothing about JESUS. She was talking to someone in the dark. She had it like this. I said, “Mom?” I went like this to her [gesture] and said, “Mom, what are you doing?” But she didn’t talk to me. So when she was done, she told him thank you, whoever it was. I was looking around to see who she was talking to. I thought I was hallucinating. There was nobody. She said, “When you get up in the morning, little one, you are not going to get sick anymore.” That is the last time I have been sick. Yeah, and I was like seven. I told Mom what I seen. She said, “Go to sleep.” So I went back to sleep. I woke up early in the morning and the chickens were crowing. Then I woke up Mom. I said, “Mom, Mom.” She said, “What is it, little one?” She grabbed me and started touching me. She said, “Gaw! You got healed!” I haven’t been sick since and that’s like 50-something years ago. I get a cold, but a fever, never.

english_text: It was pretty good back then. Based on what I know that I say it was good back then. People were important to one another, enjoyed [one] another, had humorous conversations. But, as time went on, I began to see it change. The value of things made it hard for us—on the price of things, about money. But as far as the mind and the way of thinking, it was better than the value of anything. But, nowadays, the price of things is really hard on us. The reason is people have moved from the way that they believed. And how man should walk here on this earth, with his own strength, and gather good to prosper. The way I see it, their own eyes have blinded them, Charlie. That’s what I see. As well as belief—they don’t believe anymore. They have nothing to do with the way we did things in the past. As far as I know, it is going to go back to that. Two different things are going to happen. I tell people, “It’s just going to be the way we are living now.” And, the other thing, is it going to be the way it was? And the way a person wants to be, and wants to live, he will choose. It will be good, or it will be sad. And it is sad, like I am saying, the things that are happening in the world is blinding the people. They are drawn to that. And the Lord that we have been provided is very joyful they are letting go of that. They feel like there is no truth. Quickly, they will think something else. That was the way it was. We were fishing, this One sitting here, I believe you know, too? But I don’t know if he knows where this is at? Do you know where Hickory Hollow is? Where the cemetery is? ‘Hickory Van Hollow’ they call it. Where the cemetery is, on the edge of the field, on this side, is where we used to live. In 1960 we had a drought. Charlie, where I am saying, I traveled that far through this field to the big Sallisaw Creek. A man named Man Hitter owned those fields. I would go across there with two buckets. There was a well there, on the creek. But in the creek there was no water—it was dry. That’s what happened. Then I done as much as could do, bending about to bring them water before it got hot. That’s the way it was when I grew up. And they washed... Back then washers did not exist. They call them ‘washing machine’ in English, they didn’t exist then. That far in the hollow, we were coming from there. They had one of those big things you put water in. They would take it that far to the big creek. I was telling this One, we are the same age, there is a rock there that has a groove in it. A hard rock there. I saw Mom for the first time, doing this. I was watching her I said, “Mom why are you beating those rocks? You are going to put holes in there.” I told her—we probably had one change of clothes. There was a rock there this big, ’kinda round. We were putting water in there for her, and she would put them [clothes] in there. And for soap—she was using that hard soap, all that. And, when she got enough, she pound them with the rocks. That’s when I thought she was going to put holes in our clothes. And, then we would help wring them out, just there on the creek, we hung clothes on the branches. While the clothes were drying we would look for our food. Crawdads, fish, and we would stick our hands under rocks. Yeah, we would just cook right there. Sometimes they would have potatoes. About this time there would be a garden, things like that, as well as onion. They would have a pan in the fire. They would boil crawdads in there. They would fry those crawdads. When they would get done, and when they were almost done, they would put the potatoes and onions, and those ‘kian’ they call them. Them elders always had those kian, hot peppers. They would cut those up. That was a good soup to drink. And crawdads fried real soft. Yeah that’s the way it was. And then, late in the evening, almost sundown, we would pack our clothes back to wear all the way back. That is the way it was back then. And, nowadays, they have washers and driers. I know they would, still won’t, feel like doing it [the laundry]—that’s the way it is. In the winter, we would cut wood to build a fire.

The reason is people have moved from the way that they believed. And how man should walk here on this earth, with his own strength, and gather good to prosper. It will be good, or it will be sad. And it is sad, like I am saying, the things that are happening in the world is blinding the people. They are drawn to that. And the Lord that we have been provided is very joyful they are letting go of that. They feel like there is no truth. Quickly, they will think something else. That was the way it was. syllabary_text: Charlie Ꮎ ᎤᎾ ᏓᏁᎸ ᏧᎧᏅᏟᏓ ᏧᏣᎢ ᏗᏝ ᏫᎦᎶᏍᎦ ᏧᎬᏅᏝᏓ ᎤᎾ ᏏᏆ ᏕᏥᏴᏓ ᎠᎭᏂ ᎤᎾᎿ ᏧᎧᏃᎾ ᏕᏡᎬ ᎠᏓ
english_text: Charlie—that hill by the house, that goes up towards arches, up the hill? I have got some hogs in a pen. There were some tsukvnoni trees there, ’long time ago. I remember it was in the year ’58. It was hot in the month of August. I don’t know if you remember, or y’all remember Wal Sul? Wal Sul was his name. That what was the name of that boy, that his house burned down, in Bunch? Harold Wayne, where Harold Wayne Asbill lives. Right about there. It was just laying right there. They used to call them ‘caboose.’ He had one like that there. And he lived in it, that Wal Sul—a stove for winter, and stove to cook with, he had them both. He wanted some wood, he ordered from my dad and grandpa. Where I am, tell you, these trees were those tsukvnoni—one rick [4' x 8' wood stack] for the cook stove, and one rick for the wood stove. We cut wood there, in the heat. They call it ‘crosscut saw’ in English. We were using one like that—it had long teeth and wooden handles on both sides. Someone would stand on this side, and the other on that side. They would work together. Me and my brothers would have difficulties when we would cut wood. Someone... because if someone is pushing down, it’s heavy to pull. It was then we would get into arguments. “Get off of it.” Really. At this time, I’m saying his name was Fish—Andrew Glass. Fish—y’all probably knew him. He had some mules and a wagon, he hauled that wood for us. I felt really good, I was glad, it was good. I felt like I was just playing around, I didn’t feel like they were working me hard. I didn’t think, “Why do I have to work?” Like I said, it felt like I was just playing around. In the evening, it was the same. I still feel the same way, Michael, I still feel the same way. I feel good, yeah.

Would get up on there, and sit and look around. We delivered that wood. He gave them half—50 cents, yeah, half. Fifty cents a rick of cook stove wood, and, for the wood stove, a quarter [25 cents]. And that’s what it was in 1958. That’s the way it was back then. Also, you could cut wood wherever. Nobody would say nothing. Nobody would come and see you. Also, there were not fences anywhere, back then, where the woods are. It wasn’t woods—that’s what I tell my family, gah-lee, when they speak in English they say ‘jungle’—that’s the way it is there, Charlie. If you remember, maybe you haven’t been there? South Bunch, across the railroad tracks, by the house, where that big field is? There was a big house there, and just over here was a huge horse barn. We came there about that time, there in Hickory Van Hollow. We just went there. I used to think we traveled a long ways. I used to think we went a long ways, when we moved. It was close by. There, where I am talking about, I would help my dad make fence posts and railroad ties. We would cut them down, so he could make posts and ties. I tell my family I have grown up. Boy, I worked hard since I was six years old. I was six years old, Charlie—I started then. But that’s the way it was then. A child wasn’t going to lay down somewhere, or be sitting somewhere, in the cold, in the heat. Where Charlie lives, we would be that far [away] on that mountain, we would come from out of that hollow. We would leave there at four in the morning. There, past where y’all live, in that corner where that gate is, we would be walking right there. It would turn daylight. We would get there—it is called ‘Two Springs.’ On the other ridge, that’s where it was. We would be coming back in the evening. We would get back to the hollow around nine the next morning. The same thing, that’s the way it was back then. That’s the kind of things he would do. He [Dad] bought that land where we live now. He paid it off, he borrowed money from the Cherokee Nation.

syllabary_text: ᏍᎩᎾ ᏳᏍᏓ ᎦᎵ charlie ᎢᎦ ᎠᎩᎸᏩᎦᏓ ᎠᎩᎩᏍᏗ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎾᏕᏅ ᎤᏬᏗᎨ ᏱᏄᎵᏍᏛᎾ ᎦᏚ ᎤᎾ yeah
english_text: That kind, gah-lee, Charlie. I really like it when it turns brown on top, yeah. They were talking about Fish. When Fish comes back, we are going plow the field. Gah-lee, I’m in a hurry for Fish to come back. I didn’t even know who it was. I don’t know if I asked every day, “Dad when is he coming back?” Just a little longer. Charlie, at that time what I’m talking about, we were all skinny, Charlie. It was pretty sad to look at me. Mom showed me a picture. That turnoff to where Wilson used to live—someone took a picture of me, right about there. I was already grown. Mom said, “Look boy.” Gah-lee, I seen a sad-looking boy. That child was bony, Michael. I was looking at him, I could see his ribs, his face was skinny. I said, “Gah-lee Mom, did this boy live or did he die?” I said to her. She started laughing. She said, “Boy that is you.” I tell them that the people were all like that, back then. This what I’m talking about. Sometime later, “Boy let’s go to the store. I have enough to buy flour, and maybe we can buy grease.” I went with him. They had those parked there, those digasvlugesgi, hand pump cars, at that crossing. He stopped and looked at it. He said, “Boy you think we can put this on the railroad tracks?” I said, “Why?” “We will drive it,” he said. I said, “What are we going to do if there is a train coming?” He said it would be a long time before one comes by. They knew when trains came by. I was afraid. When I helped him put it on there, he said, “You have to do this.” He taught me, and right in here was a wood [thing] standing there—that was the brake.

He said, “Boy, Fish is saying he coming back this Wednesday.” Gah, I don’t know if just ran around in that area. I thought, “Now we are going to raise some food.” We put it back on there, I put just on its own, with just a little brake. Was sitting there, we got off over there. Then he went around and told people, “This is what he has written. If I am in that train,he is going to start honking that horn, as he starts to go up that big hill. He is going to honk the horn for a long time, seven times. That train, before he gets to the bridge where he has it.” Gah-lee, I was in a hurry, still had about a week to go, or a week. I was in a hurry for it to be Wednesday.

english_text: Then Wednesday came. It [the train] came from this way, at four, it came from the north, going to the south, carrying passengers. I don’t know if I spent all day walking near the house thinking, “I hope he is in there. I wish that train would honk.” Gah-lee, sometimes I think about it, you know I believe I walked around, maybe around the house, most of the day. Hoping and wishing that train would start honking over there. All the people came, and his parents and others—Arthur, Wilson, everybody... George, Joe... they were sitting in the shade. I was listening. I heard it, far away there towards town. It was going, I could hear it even more. So I was tightened up, it was coming there, and it honked—it made a long honk, it let go, then another, about where the bridge is, it honked last. I was counting and just started jumping around. I got happy when it came to a stop.

phonetic_broad: aya
english_text: Me, I was maybe around eight years old. They opened it up. A soldier, clothes, a soldier stepped down. I thought he was the one that helps people. I was watching him. Everyone was standing where the door is. They let him out, then they went back that way, and there they let out two dogs—bluetick hound dogs. That was him, Fish, I never knew then. Just the next morning they left. There was a White man that lived on the mountain, Michael, this side—Jim Harris. They went after those horses and wagon, he bought two pairs. We were all up there where Fish grew up. It was late in the afternoon. I heard the sound of chains. I was looking that way, I was at the creek looking for crawdads, I seen somethings—ears they were this long [gestures]. I thought, “What is that?” It was them, those mules and a plow. They had all those things in there, and they were leading two cows for milking, and in the other wagon, ducks, chickens. They had it full in there. It started there, it was probably past noon when they came. When they untied the horses, they hooked up the turning plows. It started then, it didn’t start in the morning, it started then. That’s what I tell these living, that are my family. Boy, I miss them old ones. I miss them, there wasn’t no time for them. It didn’t matter what time. It could be midnight, if they say, “Let’s do it, let’s do it.” They was going to do it. That’s the way them elders were, they were all like that, not just certain ones. They were all like that. The last, where his mom lived down in the hollow, there is a few times that I know of, “Let’s kill a hog, it will just take us a little while. It won’t be long we will be eating fresh meat.” I know of one time, no I know of three times, it was towards midnight we killed a hog. Tsukiyasgi built a fire. He said, “It won’t take long to boil water.” We went and killed it, the water was boiling, then we scraped it, and gutted it. In just a little while we were eating meat and gravy.

english_text: Me, I was maybe around eight years old. They opened it up. A soldier, clothes, a soldier stepped down. I thought he was the one that helps people. I was watching him. Everyone was standing where the door is. They let him out, then they went back that way, and there they let out two dogs—bluetick hound dogs. That was him, Fish, I never knew then. Just the next morning they left. There was a White man that lived on the mountain, Michael, this side—Jim Harris. They went after those horses and wagon, he bought two pairs. We were all up there where Fish grew up. It was late in the afternoon. I heard the sound of chains. I was looking that way, I was at the creek looking for crawdads, I seen somethings—ears they were this long [gestures]. I thought, “What is that?” It was them, those mules and a plow. They had all those things in there, and they were leading two cows for milking, and in the other wagon, ducks, chickens. They had it full in there. It started there, it was probably past noon when they came. When they untied the horses, they hooked up the turning plows. It started then, it didn’t start in the morning, it started then. That’s what I tell these living, that are my family. Boy, I miss them old ones. I miss them, there wasn’t no time for them. It didn’t matter what time. It could be midnight, if they say, “Let’s do it, let’s do it.” They was going to do it. That’s the way them elders were, they were all like that, not just certain ones. They were all like that. The last, where his mom lived down in the hollow, there is a few times that I know of, “Let’s kill a hog, it will just take us a little while. It won’t be long we will be eating fresh meat.” I know of one time, no I know of three times, it was towards midnight we killed a hog. Tsukiyasgi built a fire. He said, “It won’t take long to boil water.” We went and killed it, the water was boiling, then we scraped it, and gutted it. In just a little while we were eating meat and gravy.

Everyone was standing where the door is. They let him out, then they went back that way, and there they let out two dogs—bluetick hound dogs. That was him, Fish, I never knew then. Just the next morning they left. There was a White man that lived on the mountain, Michael, this side—Jim Harris. They went after those horses and wagon, he bought two pairs. We were all up there where Fish grew up. It was late in the afternoon. I heard the sound of chains. I was looking that way, I was at the creek looking for crawdads, I seen somethings—ears they were this long [gestures]. I thought, “What is that?” It was them, those mules and a plow. They had all those things in there, and they were leading two cows for milking, and in the other wagon, ducks, chickens. They had it full in there. It started there, it was probably past noon when they came. When they untied the horses, they hooked up the turning plows. It started then, it didn’t start in the morning, it started then. That’s what I tell these living, that are my family. Boy, I miss them old ones. I miss them, there wasn’t no time for them. It didn’t matter what time. It could be midnight, if they say, “Let’s do it, let’s do it.” They was going to do it. That’s the way them elders were, they were all like that, not just certain ones. They were all like that. The last, where his mom lived down in the hollow, there is a few times that I know of, “Let’s kill a hog, it will just take us a little while. It won’t be long we will be eating fresh meat.” I know of one time, no I know of three times, it was towards midnight we killed a hog. Tsukiyasgi built a fire. He said, “It won’t take long to boil water.” We went and killed it, the water was boiling, then we scraped it, and gutted it. In just a little while we were eating meat and gravy.

syllabary_text: Ice Killer ᏚᏙᎥ ᏙᏳ ᎠᎩᏟᏯ ᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎿᎾ
english_text: Ice, Ice Killer was his name. He was always willing, and his mom was the same way. Like I said, everybody was, this what I’m telling y’all. There, across from where we lived, was that big house there where Fish grew up. You could see all that there was where we used to hoe crops. In that field, all the way to the creek. There wasn’t even a shrub this tall, nowhere. No shrubs, just grass. Sometimes when we go over there I think about things. I see the way it was now it’s growed up—trees are this big. You can’t tell it was a field at one time. That’s the way it is. Where the bridge is, we used to hoe there, this of the railroad tracks, on this was a waterfall. Saws used to live there, too. And, on the other side, that dam wasn’t there yet, Joe and them lived. Over there, this of [unclear] that was where that field started. All the way to the road. I tell people, “Just here where we lived, things were beautiful to look around.” And people go far away—you can just go just around here, in the forest and see beautiful things. I tell them, “The way we were put here on earth, yeah.” Now, here, the next morning, boy Charlie, I was in a hurry for it to turn daylight, so we could start back doing things. It turned daylight, I was sitting on the porch there. I was telling her, “Just yesterday tsawolvdv was making a sound.” I really like to hear a tsawolvdv making a sound. Back then, early in the morning they would make that sound, tsawolvdv. I was listening I was listening to them.

english_text: Bluebird, yeah, that’s its name—tsawolvdv. Tsawolvdahi, bluebird. Then Fish’s mom, Tsutliga, they used to call Dad ‘Hue’ short for Houston, “Hue come eat. It’s time to eat.” We would cross there when we got there. There was food on the table she had cooked. I was telling you—they brought chickens, and ducks, and cows, and they had milk there. Betty Christie is her name, she lives by the railroad crossing where we call ‘Bunch.’ There was a store there, at the time her dad had that store. And, on the other side, was another man. There they made cornmeal. The people that raised corn, like I said—horse pulled wagons. They would haul them in. They would have cornmeal made there. I forget how much when he would grind it... Maybe he would get five pounds for hisself? That’s the way it was. If you had something I needed, and if I had something and you needed it, they would just give each other—that that’s the way it was. It wasn’t about money, this. I know, if people would do that—like I said, it’s going to go back to that, and it’s going to go back to that—they could still have good lives. It would still be good, if they would help each other out. Helping each other out—that’s what it was. Back then someone would come, he would maybe have a little meat. He would bring it to you, and if you had something to give, you would give him something as he was going home. That’s the way this was. It was really good.

english_text: Like I said, we grow crops, they would can stuff, back then. There would be an apple tree on the creek, it would have lots of apples or peaches and plums. We would pick it—we would help peel, and cut up. Some they didn’t can—apples or peaches, they dried them. But, those plums, they would make jelly. I really like that jelly made from plums. We would cut those peaches and apples up, and this table cloth—we would lay those on the roof. We would put, there, the apples and peaches that we cut up. We would all be up there, we would have those sticks—tsuyoni, with leaves. Chasing the flies off all day. Sometimes someone would get off, and someone else would get up there. When evening came they would be dry. Then they would put them in bags, and hang them in the house. And, in the wintertime, they would cook that, or to make pies with. That’s the way it was. They did corn the same way. They would hang them up and dry them. We dried fish out the same way. They would put wood poles with a fork, and put one across. We would hang the fish there. When it came evening the fish were dry. They wouldn’t ruin. Nowadays, you couldn’t do that—the earth is much different now. It has changed, and continues to change. They would wrap those fish, and make soup—baked or fried fish patties. It was good. They would have onion hanging in the smokehouse. They would have onion hanging there, corn, and different things. I built a smokehouse, a place where we could preserve food, I built in the hollow. My dad helped me make the trusses. I cut them 10 foot long. I made it four corners, Charlie. I carried them on my shoulder for a long ways, Mike. I carried them a long ways, I made them. This big... the boys, my brothers, helped me.
